stem: A 6-year-old girl of Greek descent has severe anemia with target cells and a 'crew-cut' skull x-ray. Her alpha-globin mRNA is normal, but a splice-site mutation in both beta-globin genes cuts beta-globin mRNA by 75%.
oneliner: 6F + Greek + severe anemia + target cells + crew-cut skull + normal alpha mRNA + splice mutation both beta genes, beta mRNA −75% → why anemic?
ask: Which of the following best explains her anemia?

options.B: Too few beta chains, so free alpha chains pile up and damage red cell precursors
options.C: An abnormal beta chain that polymerises when deoxygenated

whyNot.A: Her **alpha-globin mRNA is normal**; that would be alpha-thalassemia
whyNot.C: That is **sickle cell disease** (HbS), a point mutation, not low production
whyNot.D: **Autoimmune hemolysis**: Coombs positive, spherocytes
whyNot.E: **Anemia of chronic disease**: needs inflammation, ferritin high, not a globin mutation

answer: Alpha/beta chain imbalance: excess free alpha chains precipitate (ineffective erythropoiesis)
why: **Beta production falls but alpha stays normal** → unpaired **alpha chains precipitate** in red cell precursors → they die in the marrow (**ineffective erythropoiesis**) and in the spleen (hemolysis).
chain: Free alpha chains precipitate in precursors
Precursors die in marrow → marrow expands (crew-cut skull)

idea.rule: In thalassemia the damage comes from the chain that is left over, not only the one that is missing.
also: Alpha-thalassemia: excess beta forms HbH (β4); excess gamma forms Hb Barts (γ4) in the fetus

stem: A 24-year-old woman has gum bleeding, scattered petechiae, and large bruises 2 weeks after a viral upper respiratory illness. Platelet count is 12,000/mm³, with normal hemoglobin and white count. The smear shows no schistocytes. PT and aPTT are normal, and the spleen is not palpable. A photomicrograph of her bone marrow aspirate is shown.
oneliner: 24F + bleeding gums, petechiae, bruises 2 wk after viral URI + platelets 12,000 + normal Hb, WBC, PT, aPTT + no schistocytes + no splenomegaly + marrow aspirate shown → mechanism?
ask: Which mechanism best explains her thrombocytopenia?

options.A: Replacement of the marrow by malignant cells
options.B: Failure of the marrow to produce all cell lines
options.C: Widespread thrombin generation consuming platelets
options.D: Microthrombi from deficient ADAMTS13 consuming platelets
options.E: Antibody-coated platelets removed by splenic macrophages

whyNot.A: **Acute leukemia**: abnormal white count, anemia, blasts
whyNot.B: **Aplastic anemia**: pancytopenia; her Hb and WBC are normal
whyNot.C: **DIC**: prolonged PT and aPTT; hers are normal
whyNot.D: **TTP**: schistocytes, anemia, kidney and neurologic signs; none here

answer: Immune destruction of platelets (IgG against GPIIb/IIIa)
why: **Isolated low platelets with normal coagulation and normal red and white cells** after a viral illness = **immune thrombocytopenia**. **IgG against GPIIb/IIIa** opsonizes platelets for **splenic macrophages**; the marrow responds with **more megakaryocytes**.

idea.rule: Low platelets with a normal or increased number of megakaryocytes mean peripheral destruction, not poor production.
also: Acute ITP in children often follows a virus and resolves
Chronic ITP in women: steroids, IVIG, splenectomy
Check HIV, HCV and SLE in adults

image.prompt: Photomicrograph of a bone marrow aspirate, Wright-Giemsa stain: a cellular field with numerous large megakaryocytes with multilobed nuclei and abundant granular cytoplasm, along with otherwise normal-looking erythroid and myeloid precursors. No blasts. No text or labels.

stem: A 2-week-old boy has had blue lips and skin since birth. Pulse oximetry reads 85% and does not rise on 100% oxygen. Arterial PaO2 is normal, hemoglobin is 15 g/dL, and red cell morphology is normal. Echocardiogram and chest film are normal. A drop of his blood on filter paper is chocolate brown and does not turn red when exposed to air.
oneliner: 2-wk M + cyanosis since birth + SpO2 85% not rising on 100% O2 + normal PaO2 + Hb 15 + normal smear, echo, chest film + blood chocolate brown, unchanged in air → mechanism?
ask: Which mechanism best explains his cyanosis?

options.A: Heme iron oxidized to the ferric state that cannot carry oxygen
options.C: Polymerization of deoxygenated hemoglobin
options.D: Destruction of red cells by hemolysis

whyNot.B: Echo is **normal**, and a shunt would not change the blood's brown color
whyNot.C: **Sickle cell**: smear abnormal, and symptoms start after fetal hemoglobin falls
whyNot.D: His **hemoglobin and smear are normal**, with no anemia
whyNot.E: **CO poisoning**: cherry-red blood, normal saturation reading on oximetry

answer: Methemoglobinemia (Fe3+ hemoglobin)
why: **Normal heart, lungs, PaO2, and hemoglobin** with **cyanosis unresponsive to oxygen** and **chocolate-brown blood** = methemoglobin. Heme **Fe2+ is oxidized to Fe3+**, which **cannot bind oxygen** and **shifts the curve left**, so tissues are deprived.
chain: Fe2+ in heme oxidized to Fe3+
Remaining heme binds O2 more tightly (left shift)

idea.rule: Cyanosis with normal PaO2, normal heart and lungs, and brown blood means methemoglobinemia.
also: Congenital: NADH-methemoglobin reductase deficiency
Acquired: dapsone, nitrates, benzocaine, nitrites
Treat with methylene blue or vitamin C

stem: A 29-year-old woman has had heavy menstrual bleeding since her first period, plus frequent nosebleeds and easy bruising. Her mother had the same problems. Platelet count is normal and bleeding time is prolonged. The aPTT is mildly prolonged, and the ristocetin-induced platelet response is reduced, with normal aggregation to ADP and collagen.
oneliner: 29F + menorrhagia since menarche + nosebleeds, bruising + mother similar + normal platelet count + long bleeding time + mild aPTT prolongation + low ristocetin response, normal ADP and collagen aggregation → which step fails?
ask: Which step of hemostasis is most impaired?

options.A: Platelet aggregation by fibrinogen bridging through GPIIb/IIIa
options.B: Platelet adhesion to exposed subendothelium via GPIb
options.C: Release of platelet granule contents
options.D: Conversion of fibrinogen to cross-linked fibrin

whyNot.A: Normal **ADP and collagen aggregation** shows aggregation is intact (this is Glanzmann)
whyNot.C: Granule release would give **abnormal collagen aggregation**; hers is normal
whyNot.D: A defect gives **delayed or deep bleeding**, with normal bleeding time
whyNot.E: Would give a **markedly prolonged PT and aPTT**, not isolated platelet-type bleeding

answer: Adhesion failure from deficient von Willebrand factor (von Willebrand disease)
why: **Mucocutaneous bleeding with normal platelet count, long bleeding time, and low ristocetin response** = **von Willebrand disease**. vWF **links GPIb on platelets to subendothelial collagen**, so adhesion fails; it also **carries factor VIII**, explaining the mild aPTT rise.
chain: Factor VIII also low, aPTT rises

idea.rule: vWF bridges platelet GPIb to collagen (adhesion) and protects factor VIII.
also: Desmopressin releases stored vWF
Bernard-Soulier: GPIb defect, ristocetin does not correct with normal plasma
Glanzmann: GPIIb/IIIa defect, no aggregation

stem: Platelet-rich plasma from a healthy volunteer is placed in a light-transmittance aggregometer. An agonist added at 5 µM causes platelets to change shape and aggregate rapidly and irreversibly, and light transmission climbs sharply. Platelets from a patient taking clopidogrel show only weak, reversible aggregation with the same agonist, while their response to arachidonic acid is normal.
oneliner: Aggregometry + 5 µM agonist → fast irreversible aggregation + blunted by clopidogrel, normal arachidonic acid response → which agonist?
ask: Which reagent was most likely added?

options.C: Ristocetin

whyNot.A: Acts mainly through **GPVI and α2β1**; its response is not the one defined by P2Y12 blockade
whyNot.B: Converted by **COX-1 to thromboxane A2**, blocked by **aspirin**; the stem says this response is **normal**
whyNot.C: Causes **agglutination via vWF binding GPIb**, independent of P2Y12; used to test von Willebrand disease
whyNot.E: Acts through **PAR-1**; a potent agonist not blocked by clopidogrel

answer: ADP via P2Y12 activates GPIIb/IIIa
why: **ADP binds P2Y12** (blocked by clopidogrel) and P2Y1. Gi signalling lowers cAMP and **activates GPIIb/IIIa**, so fibrinogen cross-links platelets into a strong, irreversible second-wave aggregate.
chain: Gi signalling lowers cAMP, shape change

idea.rule: ADP acting through P2Y12 amplifies platelet activation, and clopidogrel, prasugrel and ticagrelor block this receptor.
also: Prasugrel and ticlopidine: irreversible P2Y12 blockers like clopidogrel
Ticagrelor and IV cangrelor: reversible P2Y12 blockers
Clopidogrel is a prodrug activated by CYP2C19; poor metabolizers respond less
Dense granules release ADP, so P2Y12 blockade also weakens responses to other agonists

stem: A 34-year-old man nicks his lip while shaving. Within seconds the bleeding slows noticeably, well before any clot can be seen.
oneliner: 34M + shaving cut + bleeding slows within seconds, before any clot → what acts first?
ask: Which event is most responsible for the rapid early slowing of bleeding?

options.B: Platelet plug formed by GPIIb/IIIa bridging
options.C: Fibrin polymerization
options.E: Cleavage of prothrombin by factor Xa

whyNot.B: Plug builds over about **1 to 3 minutes**, not seconds
whyNot.C: The **last, slowest** step (minutes) that stabilises the plug
whyNot.D: An **anticoagulant**; it limits clotting, it does not stop bleeding
whyNot.E: Generates thrombin over **minutes**, after the platelet plug

answer: Reflex neurogenic spasm plus endothelin release constrict the injured vessel
why: Injured endothelium and a neurogenic reflex cause **immediate vasoconstriction** (endothelin released). Flow falls within seconds, buying time for the **platelet plug** and then fibrin.

idea.rule: Hemostasis order: vasoconstriction first, then the platelet plug (primary), then fibrin (secondary).
also: Platelet adhesion needs vWF binding GPIb
Fibrin from the coagulation cascade stabilises the plug over minutes
Endothelial PGI2 and NO keep the plug limited to the injury

stem: A 58-year-old woman with refractory rheumatoid arthritis for 10 years has fatigue and pallor. Hemoglobin is 9.6 g/dL and MCV is 78 fL. Serum iron is low, total iron-binding capacity is low and ferritin is 250 ng/mL. A Prussian blue stain of a bone marrow aspirate is shown.
oneliner: 58F + 10 y RA + anemia, MCV 78 + low iron, low TIBC, ferritin 250 + Prussian blue marrow shown → why anemic?
ask: Which of the following best explains her anemia?

options.A: Chronic blood loss from NSAID-induced gastritis
options.B: Inflammation raises hepcidin, so iron is trapped in macrophages
options.C: Replacement of marrow by tumor or fibrosis
options.D: Ring sideroblasts from impaired mitochondrial heme synthesis

whyNot.A: That would give **low ferritin, high TIBC and absent marrow iron**
whyNot.C: **Myelophthisis** gives teardrop cells and leukoerythroblastic smear
whyNot.D: **Sideroblastic anemia** has **high** serum iron and ferritin with ringed erythroblasts
whyNot.E: **Beta-thalassemia** has normal iron indices and target cells

answer: Hepcidin blocks ferroportin so macrophages hold iron
why: **IL-6** from chronic inflammation raises **hepcidin**, which blocks **ferroportin**. Iron stays inside macrophages (**stainable marrow iron**) but is **unavailable** for erythropoiesis, so serum iron and TIBC are low and ferritin high.
chain: Ferroportin blocked, iron stuck in macrophages
Low serum iron, low TIBC, high ferritin

idea.rule: Anemia of chronic disease has low serum iron but plentiful stored iron; iron deficiency has both low.
also: Iron deficiency: low ferritin, high TIBC, absent marrow iron
Treat the underlying disease; EPO may help
Hepcidin also limits iron from bacteria during infection

image.prompt: Prussian blue stain of a bone marrow aspirate: abundant blue-staining iron granules within marrow macrophages, with scattered developing red cells; no ringed erythroblasts. No text or labels.

stem: A 72-year-old man has had 4 months of fatigue and breathlessness on climbing stairs, and looks pale. Hemoglobin is 8.4 g/dL and MCV is 71 fL. White cell and platelet counts are normal. A peripheral blood smear is shown.
oneliner: 72M + fatigue + pallor + Hb 8.4, MCV 71 + normal WBC and platelets + smear shown → why anemic?
ask: Which of the following best explains his anemia?

options.C: Impaired DNA synthesis from vitamin B12 deficiency
options.D: Chronic gastrointestinal blood loss depleting iron

whyNot.A: **Aplastic anemia** causes **pancytopenia**; his WBC and platelets are normal
whyNot.B: **CML** raises the **white count**; it is not microcytic
whyNot.C: Gives **macrocytic** cells, not MCV 71
whyNot.E: **Beta-thalassemia major** presents in infancy, not at 72

answer: Occult GI bleeding depletes iron and impairs heme synthesis
why: A **hypochromic, microcytic** picture in an older man means **iron deficiency** until proven otherwise. Slow **GI bleeding** (e.g. colon cancer) uses up iron, so **heme and hemoglobin synthesis fall** and red cells come out small and pale.

idea.rule: New iron deficiency in an older man or postmenopausal woman means GI blood loss, until proven otherwise.
also: Look for colon cancer (colonoscopy)
Iron deficiency in children: diet; in young women: menses
Pencil cells and low ferritin support the diagnosis

image.prompt: Peripheral blood smear: numerous small red blood cells with enlarged central pallor (hypochromic microcytes) and occasional elongated pencil-shaped cells; white cells and platelets look normal. No text or labels.

stem: A 52-year-old woman with chronic myeloid leukemia has progressed to blast crisis with 60% marrow blasts. She does not respond to mitoxantrone plus vinblastine. Plasma drug levels are in the therapeutic range, but drug is almost undetectable inside her blasts. Liver and kidney function are normal.
oneliner: 52F + CML in blast crisis, 60% blasts + no response to mitoxantrone and vinblastine + therapeutic plasma levels but almost none inside blasts + normal liver and kidney → mechanism of resistance?
ask: Which mechanism most likely explains the resistance?

options.C: Binding of drug to plasma proteins
options.D: Overexpression of an ATP-dependent efflux pump (P-glycoprotein) in the blasts
options.E: A kinase-domain mutation in the drug target (T315I)

whyNot.A: Plasma levels are **therapeutic**, so systemic clearance is not the problem
whyNot.B: Same point: **plasma levels are fine**, and kidney function is normal
whyNot.C: Would change **plasma** free drug, not selectively lower the level inside blasts
whyNot.E: Resistance to **imatinib-type** drugs; it would not lower **intracellular** concentration of these agents

answer: MDR1 overexpression: P-glycoprotein pumps the drugs out of the leukemic cells
why: **Normal plasma levels but low drug inside the cells** means the cells are exporting it. **MDR1 gene amplification or overexpression** raises **P-glycoprotein**, an ATP-driven pump that expels many chemotherapy drugs.
chain: Selection of clones with high MDR1

idea.rule: Resistance with normal plasma but low intracellular drug = efflux pump (MDR1/P-glycoprotein).
also: Drugs pumped: anthracyclines, vinca alkaloids, taxanes, etoposide
Also found in normal gut, liver, kidney and blood-brain barrier cells
Verapamil and similar drugs can inhibit the pump

stem: A 45-year-old woman has 3 weeks of fever and easy bruising. White cell count is 150,000/µL with many myelocytes, metamyelocytes and neutrophils at all stages of maturity, and marrow cytogenetics show a translocation between chromosomes 9 and 22.
oneliner: 45F + fever, bruising + WBC 150,000 with immature neutrophils at all stages + t(9;22) → what drives the proliferation?
ask: Which molecular event most likely drives her cell proliferation?

options.A: A point mutation in the ABL gene
options.B: A point mutation in the BCR gene
options.C: A fusion gene encoding a constitutively active tyrosine kinase
options.E: Loss of retinoblastoma protein by promoter methylation

whyNot.A: The translocation joins two genes; it is **not a point mutation**
whyNot.B: The translocation **fuses BCR with ABL1**; a point change in BCR alone would not create a kinase
whyNot.D: Seen in **progression**, not the initiating event of this disease
whyNot.E: Not linked to a 9;22 translocation

answer: BCR-ABL1 fusion: constitutive tyrosine kinase activity (chronic myeloid leukemia)
why: **t(9;22)** fuses **BCR to ABL1**. The fusion protein is a **constitutively active tyrosine kinase** that drives myeloid proliferation independent of growth signals. It is the target of **imatinib**.
chain: t(9;22) in a myeloid stem cell

idea.rule: A recurrent translocation usually creates a fusion gene, not a point mutation.
also: t(14;18): BCL2 overexpression in follicular lymphoma
t(8;14): MYC overexpression in Burkitt lymphoma
t(15;17): PML-RARA in acute promyelocytic leukemia
t(11;22): EWSR1-FLI1 in Ewing sarcoma

stem: A 34-year-old man has 4 weeks of dyspnea on exertion and looks pale. On room air his PaO2 is 98 mmHg, PaCO2 40 mmHg, and hemoglobin is 6.5 g/dL.
oneliner: 34M + exertional dyspnea + pallor + PaO2 98, PaCO2 40 + Hb 6.5 → why breathless?
ask: Which mechanism best explains his dyspnea?

options.C: Reduced oxygen-carrying capacity lowers arterial oxygen content despite normal PaO2

whyNot.A: **PaCO2 is normal**, so ventilation is adequate
whyNot.B: Would lower **PaO2**; his is normal
whyNot.D: PaO2 of 98 shows he is **oxygenating normally**
whyNot.E: PaCO2 is **normal**, so no respiratory alkalosis

answer: Anemia lowers oxygen content (Hb-bound O2), not PaO2
why: Oxygen content is **mostly hemoglobin-bound** (1.34 x Hb x SaO2). With **Hb 6.5 and normal PaO2**, content falls by half while **PaO2 and saturation stay normal**, so tissues are under-supplied and he is breathless on effort.

idea.rule: Anemia lowers oxygen content, not PaO2 or saturation.
also: Carbon monoxide poisoning: normal PaO2, low true saturation
Methemoglobinemia: normal PaO2, low content
Hypoxemic causes (V/Q mismatch, hypoventilation) lower PaO2

stem: A 33-year-old woman has had 2 days of fever, headache and confusion, with dark urine. Hemoglobin is 7.8 g/dL, platelets 18,000/µL, creatinine 2.4 mg/dL, LDH is high, haptoglobin is low, and PT and PTT are normal. She has had no diarrhea and has not received heparin. A peripheral blood smear is shown.
oneliner: 33F + fever + confusion + dark urine + Hb 7.8 + platelets 18k + creatinine 2.4 + high LDH, low haptoglobin + normal PT and PTT + no diarrhea or heparin + smear shown → underlying defect?
ask: Which abnormality most likely underlies her illness?

options.A: Shiga toxin injury to renal endothelium
options.B: Consumption of fibrinogen after tissue factor release
options.C: Antibodies to platelet factor 4–heparin complexes
options.E: Deficiency of ADAMTS13 with ultra-large von Willebrand factor multimers

whyNot.A: Follows **bloody diarrhea**, which she did not have
whyNot.B: **DIC** prolongs PT and PTT; hers are normal
whyNot.C: She has **no heparin exposure**, and it does not cause hemolysis
whyNot.D: **ITP** has isolated low platelets without hemolysis or renal failure

answer: ADAMTS13 deficiency leading to ultra-large vWF multimers and platelet microthrombi (TTP)
why: **Fever, neurologic change, renal failure, hemolytic anemia with schistocytes and thrombocytopenia, and normal PT/PTT** point to **TTP**. **Missing ADAMTS13** leaves **ultra-large vWF multimers** that make **platelet-rich microthrombi** in small vessels, shearing red cells.

idea.rule: Microangiopathic hemolysis with low platelets and normal PT/PTT = TTP or HUS, not DIC.
also: Autoantibody to ADAMTS13 in most acquired cases
Treatment: plasma exchange and immunosuppression
HUS: Shiga toxin, kidneys prominent

image.prompt: Peripheral blood smear at high power showing many fragmented red cells (schistocytes, helmet cells and triangular cells), polychromasia and very few platelets, no text or labels.

stem: A 58-year-old man with colon cancer metastatic to the liver responds well to chemotherapy at first. Two years later the metastases enlarge faster and no longer respond to drugs that worked before. Biopsy of the recurrent lesions shows many more mutations than the primary tumor.
oneliner: 58M + colon cancer with liver metastases + early chemo response + later faster growth and resistance + biopsy with many more mutations than primary → mechanism of progression?
ask: Which mechanism best explains the change in tumor behavior?

options.C: Genomic instability with accumulating mutations and selection of aggressive clones
options.D: Overexpression of p15, p16 and p18
options.E: Overexpression of p21, p27 and p57

whyNot.A: Would **slow** mitosis, not speed growth
whyNot.B: Hypophosphorylated RB **blocks** the cell cycle
whyNot.D: These **CDK inhibitors** slow the cycle
whyNot.E: These are **cell-cycle brakes**, and would not add mutations

answer: Clonal evolution driven by genomic instability
why: Cancers with **defective DNA repair or checkpoint control** keep **mutating**. **Treatment and the microenvironment select** subclones that **grow faster, invade and resist drugs**, so the tumor changes as it progresses.

idea.rule: Tumor progression is evolution: instability makes variants, selection keeps the fittest.
also: Mismatch repair defects (Lynch): microsatellite instability
p53 loss lets damaged cells keep dividing
Multiple-hit accumulation in adenoma to carcinoma sequence

stem: A 24-year-old man received chemotherapy for lymphoma 10 days ago. He now has multiple pinpoint, flat, nonblanching red spots on his shins and along the belt line, with no large bruises or joint swelling. PT and PTT are normal. A photograph of his legs is shown.
oneliner: 24M + 10 d after chemotherapy for lymphoma + pinpoint nonblanching red spots on shins and belt line + no large bruises or joint swelling + normal PT and PTT + photo shown → what process?
ask: Which process most likely explains the skin lesions?

options.B: Reduced hepatic synthesis of clotting factors
options.C: Protein C deficiency
options.D: Failure of primary hemostasis from too few platelets made by the marrow
options.E: Loss of vascular support from vitamin C deficiency

whyNot.A: Gives **palpable** purpura, not flat spots
whyNot.B: Would give **prolonged PT** and larger bruises or hematomas
whyNot.C: Causes **painful necrotic skin lesions** after warfarin, not petechiae
whyNot.E: Gives **perifollicular** hemorrhages and corkscrew hairs, with no chemotherapy link

answer: Marrow suppression leading to thrombocytopenia and petechiae
why: Chemotherapy **suppresses megakaryocytes**, so **few platelets** are made. Without platelet plugs, **small skin vessels leak red cells** as **petechiae**; coagulation tests stay normal.

idea.rule: Petechiae mean a platelet problem; factor deficiencies cause deep bleeds and joint bleeding.
also: ITP: increased destruction, normal marrow
Mucosal bleeding and epistaxis accompany low platelets
Coagulation factor defects: hemarthroses, prolonged PT or PTT

image.prompt: Photograph of an adult's lower legs below the knee, skin clothed above the knee, showing many scattered pinpoint 1-mm flat red-purple nonblanching macules, no text or labels.

stem: A 63-year-old woman has had 2 months of back pain and fatigue. Calcium is 13.4 mg/dL, PTH is suppressed, PTH-related peptide is undetectable, and 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D is low. She takes no medications. There is tenderness over T6, a serum monoclonal spike, and lytic lesions on x-ray.
oneliner: 63F + back pain + fatigue + Ca 13.4 + low PTH, PTHrP undetectable, low 1,25-vitamin D + no medications + T6 tenderness + monoclonal spike + lytic lesions → cause of hypercalcemia?
ask: Which mechanism most likely explains the hypercalcemia?

options.C: Increased intestinal absorption driven by 1,25-vitamin D
options.D: Tumor-derived cytokines stimulating osteoclast bone resorption
options.E: Increased renal calcium reabsorption from a thiazide

whyNot.A: PTH is **suppressed**
whyNot.B: It is **undetectable**
whyNot.C: 1,25-vitamin D is **low**
whyNot.E: She takes **no medications**

answer: Local cytokines (IL-1, IL-6, TNF, RANKL) from myeloma cells activate osteoclasts
why: **Multiple myeloma** plasma cells release **IL-1, IL-6, TNF and RANKL-inducing signals**, which **activate osteoclasts**. The result is **lytic bone lesions and hypercalcemia** with **suppressed PTH**.

idea.rule: Hypercalcemia of malignancy: PTHrP (solid tumors), cytokine osteolysis (myeloma), 1,25-vitamin D (lymphoma).
also: Squamous cell cancers: PTHrP
Hodgkin and non-Hodgkin lymphomas: 1,25-vitamin D
Bone metastases from breast cancer

stem: A 6-year-old girl has chronic hemolytic anemia with splenomegaly. Pyruvate kinase is purified from her red cells and from a control. At saturating phosphoenolpyruvate both reach the same maximal velocity, but her enzyme needs a much higher substrate concentration to reach half-maximal velocity.
oneliner: 6F + chronic hemolysis + splenomegaly + purified red cell pyruvate kinase: same Vmax as control but needs much more PEP for half-maximal rate → what changed?
ask: Which change in the enzyme best explains the findings?

options.B: Decreased turnover number of each molecule
options.C: Fewer enzyme molecules from low synthesis or fast degradation

whyNot.B: Would also **lower Vmax**
whyNot.C: Would **lower Vmax**, and her Vmax is the same
whyNot.D: Would **lower Vmax** with unchanged Km; the enzyme is purified
whyNot.E: Would need **less** substrate, not more

answer: Mutant pyruvate kinase with higher Km: less glycolytic ATP and hemolysis
why: **Same Vmax but a rightward shift** means the enzyme works as well when saturated but binds substrate poorly: **higher Km**. Red cells must **make ATP by glycolysis**; **pyruvate kinase** produces it, so **ATP falls, membrane pumps fail** and cells are removed by the spleen.
chain: Glycolytic ATP falls in red cells

idea.rule: Km reflects affinity (higher Km = lower affinity); Vmax reflects amount of working enzyme.
also: Competitive inhibitor: higher apparent Km, same Vmax
Noncompetitive inhibitor: lower Vmax, same Km
Red cells have no mitochondria, so depend on glycolysis

stem: A 27-year-old woman has dark urine in the morning on and off for a year, with fatigue and abdominal pain. Hemoglobin is 8.1 g/dL, LDH is raised, haptoglobin is low, and indirect bilirubin is increased. The direct Coombs test is negative. An acidified serum test causes her red cells to lyse. The smear shows no spherocytes and no Heinz bodies, and the MCV is normal.
oneliner: 27F + morning dark urine + fatigue, abdominal pain + Hb 8.1, high LDH, low haptoglobin + Coombs negative + acid serum test positive + no spherocytes or Heinz bodies → mechanism of hemolysis?
ask: Which of the following best explains her hemolysis?

options.A: Missing membrane inhibitors of complement on red cells
options.C: Defect in red cell cytoskeletal proteins

whyNot.B: Would show **Heinz bodies and bite cells** after oxidant exposure
whyNot.C: Gives **spherocytes** with a raised MCHC; none are seen
whyNot.D: Gives **microcytosis** (low MCV)
whyNot.E: The **Coombs test is negative**

answer: PNH: PIGA mutation, no GPI-anchored CD55 and CD59, complement-mediated lysis
why: A **PIGA mutation** in a stem cell prevents GPI anchor synthesis, so red cells lack **CD55 and CD59**. **Complement acts unchecked**, causing **intravascular hemolysis** and hemoglobinuria, often visible at night when blood pH falls slightly.
chain: Somatic PIGA mutation in a stem cell
No GPI anchors on cell surface

idea.rule: Missing CD55/CD59 on a GPI anchor means complement-mediated intravascular hemolysis.
also: Diagnosis: flow cytometry for CD55 and CD59
Thrombosis is a major cause of death (hepatic vein)
Treat with eculizumab or ravulizumab (anti-C5)
Can progress to aplastic anemia

stem: A 67-year-old man with chronic lymphocytic leukemia has two days of fatigue and yellow eyes. Hemoglobin has dropped from 12.1 to 7.4 g/dL, reticulocytes are 8%, indirect bilirubin and LDH are raised, and haptoglobin is low. Platelet count is normal. A peripheral blood smear is shown.
oneliner: 67M + CLL + sudden anemia + retics 8% + high indirect bilirubin and LDH + low haptoglobin + normal platelets + smear shown → why anemic?
ask: Which process best explains his anemia?

options.A: Antibody-coated red cells removed by splenic macrophages
options.B: Leukemic cells crowding out the marrow
options.C: Marrow stem cell failure
options.E: Mechanical shearing of red cells on fibrin strands

whyNot.B: Marrow infiltration gives a **low reticulocyte count**; his retics are 8%
whyNot.C: **Aplastic anemia**: reticulocytes low, and no hemolysis markers
whyNot.D: **Iron deficiency**: microcytic, low retics, no jaundice
whyNot.E: **Microangiopathy**: schistocytes with low platelets; his **platelets are normal**

answer: Warm autoimmune hemolysis: IgG-coated cells lose membrane in the spleen
why: CLL B cells are dysregulated and can make **IgG autoantibodies against red cells**. Splenic macrophages bite off membrane, leaving **spherocytes**, and the **hemolysis** gives high retics, indirect bilirubin and low haptoglobin.

idea.rule: High reticulocytes plus indirect bilirubin means hemolysis, not marrow failure.
also: Warm AIHA: IgG, spleen; CLL, SLE, methyldopa
Cold AIHA: IgM, complement; Mycoplasma, EBV
Hereditary spherocytosis and G6PD deficiency: same high retics and indirect bilirubin

image.prompt: Peripheral blood smear, high power, showing many small dense round red cells without central pallor (spherocytes) mixed with larger bluish polychromatic cells; a few small mature lymphocytes in the background. No text or labels.

stem: A 33-year-old woman at 30 weeks of pregnancy is started on unfractionated heparin for a deep vein thrombosis. Her platelet count was 220,000/mm3 at baseline and falls to 44,000/mm3 on day 7, with new swelling in the other leg. Her spleen is not enlarged, and she has no bleeding, no new drugs and no infection.
oneliner: 33F + 30 weeks pregnant + heparin for DVT + platelets 220k to 44k by day 7 + new leg swelling + no bleeding → mechanism?
ask: Which mechanism best explains the platelet fall?

options.A: Antibodies against megakaryocytes in the marrow
options.C: Sequestration in an enlarged spleen
options.E: IgG against heparin-platelet factor 4 complexes activating platelets

whyNot.A: **Amegakaryocytic** process: no thrombosis and not heparin-timed
whyNot.B: No large fluid load and it would **not cause new thrombosis**
whyNot.C: **Hypersplenism**: needs splenomegaly; **her spleen is normal**, and no heparin timing
whyNot.D: **ITP**: bleeding rather than thrombosis, and no exposure-timed drop

answer: Heparin-PF4 immune complexes activate platelets, causing consumption and thrombosis
why: Heparin binds **platelet factor 4**, and IgG against the **heparin-PF4 complex** binds platelet Fc receptors. Platelets **activate and aggregate**, so the count falls (usually day 5 to 10) while **thrombosis** develops: low platelets with clots.

idea.rule: Antibodies against heparin-PF4 activate platelets, so the count falls while clots form.
also: Classic HIT: day 5 to 10 after starting heparin
Rapid HIT within a day if heparin was given in the past 100 days
Vaccine-induced thrombotic thrombocytopenia: anti-PF4 without heparin

stem: A 7-day-old boy born at home has oozing from the umbilical stump and bruising. He is exclusively breastfed, is otherwise well, and was given no injection at birth. PT and aPTT are prolonged, platelet count and fibrinogen are normal, and the mother has no family bleeding history.
oneliner: 7-day-old boy + home birth, no injection + exclusively breastfed + umbilical oozing + long PT and aPTT + normal platelets and fibrinogen → defective process?
ask: Which biochemical process is defective?

options.B: Gamma-carboxylation of glutamate residues on clotting factors
options.C: Cross-linking of collagen by lysyl oxidase
options.E: Binding of factor VIII to von Willebrand factor

whyNot.A: **Scurvy**: fragile vessels with normal PT and aPTT
whyNot.C: **Copper deficiency**: weak connective tissue, not a prolonged PT
whyNot.D: **Folate deficiency**: macrocytic anemia, not bleeding with a long PT
whyNot.E: **vWD or hemophilia A**: isolated long aPTT and a family history

answer: Vitamin K deficiency stops gamma-carboxylation of factors II, VII, IX, X
why: **Vitamin K** is the cofactor for **gamma-carboxylation of glutamate** on factors **II, VII, IX, X** (and proteins C and S). Newborns have **sterile guts and little in breast milk**, so without prophylaxis the factors are inactive and **both PT and aPTT lengthen**.
chain: Low stores, sterile gut, breast milk low
Factors II, VII, IX, X not carboxylated

idea.rule: Vitamin K carboxylates glutamate on factors II, VII, IX, X (and C and S).
also: Warfarin blocks vitamin K epoxide reductase
Late bleeding at 2 to 12 weeks if prophylaxis missed
Broad-spectrum antibiotics reduce gut vitamin K

stem: A 46-year-old man is admitted after a withdrawal seizure and drinks a pint of whiskey daily. Hemoglobin is 8.9 g/dL, MCV is 112 fL, reticulocytes are low, and WBC is 3.1. Vitamin B12 and methylmalonic acid are normal. A peripheral blood smear is shown.
oneliner: 46M + heavy alcohol + withdrawal seizure + Hb 8.9, MCV 112 + low retics + WBC 3.1 + normal B12 and MMA + smear shown → process?
ask: Which process underlies his anemia?

options.C: Impaired DNA synthesis from lack of thymidylate production
options.E: Failure of stem cells in the marrow

whyNot.A: **Thalassemia**: microcytic, with a normal or raised cell count and target cells
whyNot.B: **Iron deficiency or lead**: microcytic or normocytic; his MCV is 112
whyNot.D: **Hemolysis**: high retics, spherocytes; his retics are low
whyNot.E: **Aplastic anemia**: hypocellular marrow, **no hypersegmented neutrophils** or macro-ovalocytes

answer: Folate deficiency impairs thymidylate synthesis and DNA replication, producing megaloblastic anemia
why: Alcohol use causes **poor intake and malabsorption of folate**, plus direct marrow toxicity. Without folate, **thymidylate (dTMP) synthesis fails**, so **DNA replication lags behind RNA and protein synthesis** in marrow precursors and cells become large with **hypersegmented neutrophils**.

idea.rule: Anything that blocks thymidylate (DNA) synthesis gives megaloblastic cells and hypersegmented neutrophils.
also: B12 deficiency: same smear plus raised methylmalonic acid and neuropathy
Methotrexate and trimethoprim block dihydrofolate reductase
Hydroxyurea and 5-FU block DNA synthesis

image.prompt: Peripheral blood smear, high power, showing many large oval red cells (macro-ovalocytes) with a hypersegmented neutrophil (six lobes) in the center. No text or labels.

stem: A 27-year-old woman at 32 weeks of an uncomplicated pregnancy has no symptoms. Hemoglobin is 10.4 g/dL with MCV 90 fL and normal ferritin and reticulocytes. The direct antiglobulin test is negative and there is no bleeding.
oneliner: 27F + 32 weeks, uncomplicated + asymptomatic + Hb 10.4 + MCV 90 + normal ferritin and retics + Coombs negative → mechanism?
ask: Which mechanism best explains her hemoglobin?

options.A: Plasma volume rising more than red cell mass
options.C: Impaired DNA synthesis from folate lack

whyNot.B: **Hemolysis**: the antiglobulin test is negative and retics are normal
whyNot.C: **Megaloblastic**: MCV would be above 100
whyNot.D: No bleeding or symptoms, and **ferritin is normal**
whyNot.E: Erythropoietin **rises** in pregnancy; red cell mass increases

answer: Hemodilution: plasma volume expands by about 50% while red cells increase by about 25%
why: Pregnancy raises **plasma volume by about 50%** and red cell mass by only **about 25%**, so Hb and hematocrit fall by **dilution**. With normal MCV, ferritin and retics, this is **physiologic**, not a true deficiency.
chain: Mild normocytic anemia, normal iron studies

idea.rule: Mild normocytic anemia in a healthy pregnancy is dilutional.
also: Serum albumin also falls by dilution
Hb and hematocrit fall most in the second trimester
True iron deficiency instead shows low ferritin and low MCV

stem: A 61-year-old woman who has never smoked has lung adenocarcinoma. Tumour sequencing shows an activating mutation in the gene for epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR).
oneliner: 61F nonsmoker + lung adenocarcinoma + activating EGFR mutation → how does this receptor signal?
ask: The normal product of the mutated gene belongs to which receptor class?

options.A: Receptor associated with cytoplasmic JAK kinases
options.B: Receptor with intrinsic guanylyl cyclase activity
options.C: Receptor with intrinsic serine/threonine kinase activity
options.D: Receptor with intrinsic tyrosine kinase activity
options.E: Receptor coupled to heterotrimeric G protein

whyNot.A: Cytokine receptors (EPO, IL-2) lack their own kinase and borrow **JAKs**; EGFR has its own kinase domain
whyNot.B: Makes **cGMP** (e.g. ANP receptor), not phosphotyrosine
whyNot.C: Phosphorylates **Ser/Thr** (e.g. TGF-beta receptor), not tyrosine
whyNot.E: Signal through **G proteins** and second messengers, no dimer cross-phosphorylation

answer: Receptor tyrosine kinase
why: EGFR and PDGFR are **receptor tyrosine kinases**. Ligand binding causes **dimerisation and autophosphorylation of tyrosines**, which recruit adaptors that activate the **Ras-MAPK** and PI3K pathways.

idea.rule: Receptor tyrosine kinases dimerise and autophosphorylate; overactive ones drive cancer.
also: EGFR (lung cancer)
PDGFR
VEGFR
Insulin receptor and IGF-1 receptor
RET and KIT

stem: A 3-year-old boy has white pupillary reflexes in both eyes. A tumour is found in each eye, and in the tumour cells both copies of a gene on chromosome 13q14 are inactivated.
oneliner: 3M + bilateral white pupillary reflex + both copies of a 13q14 gene lost in tumour → normal gene product does what?
ask: What is the normal function of the product of the inactivated gene?

options.A: Drives cell-cycle entry as a growth factor receptor
options.B: Activates a G protein in growth-factor signalling
options.C: Blocks apoptosis by binding BAX
options.E: Restrains progression through the cell cycle

whyNot.A: This is an **oncogene** function, and oncogenes need only **one** altered copy
whyNot.B: Gain-of-function **Ras-type** signalling, a **dominant** oncogene mechanism
whyNot.C: **BCL-2** type oncogene function; it is not lost in this tumour
whyNot.D: **Mismatch repair** genes are on other chromosomes and their loss gives Lynch-type cancers, not bilateral eye tumours

answer: Restrains progression through the cell cycle (tumour suppressor)
why: RB1 encodes a **tumour suppressor** whose product (**Rb**) holds cells in **G1** until growth signals arrive. Loss of **both alleles** removes the brake, so cells proliferate without restraint.
chain: Normal Rb brakes the G1 to S transition

idea.rule: Tumour suppressors brake growth (loss of both alleles); oncogenes accelerate it (one altered allele).
also: TP53 (guardian of G1/S)
APC (Wnt/beta-catenin)
BRCA1 and BRCA2
NF1 and PTEN

stem: An enzyme in liver mitochondria condenses succinyl-CoA with glycine in a pyridoxal phosphate-dependent step that is rate-limiting for its pathway.
oneliner: Liver mitochondrial enzyme + succinyl-CoA and glycine + rate-limiting, B6-dependent → end product of pathway?
ask: What is the end product of this pathway?

options.C: Urea

whyNot.A: Made from **acetyl-CoA** via HMG-CoA reductase
whyNot.C: Made in the **urea cycle** from ammonia, CO2 and aspartate
whyNot.D: Made from **cholesterol precursors** by hydroxylations
whyNot.E: Made from **glycine and arginine**, not succinyl-CoA

answer: Heme
why: **ALA synthase** joins **succinyl-CoA and glycine** (with **B6**) to make delta-aminolevulinic acid, the **rate-limiting** first step of **heme** synthesis. Heme feeds back to inhibit the enzyme.
chain: ALA continues to porphyrin ring and heme

idea.rule: ALA synthase is the rate-limiting, B6-dependent first step of heme synthesis, inhibited by heme.
also: B6 deficiency lowers heme synthesis (sideroblastic anemia)
Isoniazid causes sideroblastic anemia via B6 depletion
X-linked sideroblastic anemia from ALAS2 mutation
Heme and glucose repress hepatic ALA synthase

stem: A 6-year-old girl with acute myeloid leukemia, whose leukemic cells were 46,XX, has chemotherapy and a bone marrow transplant. Two months later her blood counts are normal and no blasts are seen, but karyotyping of circulating leukocytes shows 46,XY.
oneliner: 6F + AML (46,XX) + bone marrow transplant + 2 months later blood 46,XY, no blasts → why?
ask: Which of the following best explains the karyotype?

options.A: A disorder of sex development present since birth
options.B: Relapse of the leukemia with a new clone
options.C: Marrow from a male donor now makes her blood cells
options.D: Radiation-induced loss of an X chromosome

whyNot.A: Her karyotype was **46,XX** before transplant
whyNot.B: Normal counts and **no blasts**; a relapse clone would stay XX
whyNot.D: Cannot **gain a Y** chromosome
whyNot.E: Would give **abnormal counts** and clonal changes, not a normal XY karyotype

answer: Nonautologous (allogeneic male) donor
why: After allogeneic transplant the recipient's marrow is replaced by **donor stem cells**, so circulating blood cells carry the **donor's karyotype** (**chimerism**). A **Y** chromosome in a girl means the donor was male.
chain: Donor cells make all blood lineages

idea.rule: After allogeneic transplant, blood cells carry the donor's genotype (chimerism).
also: Female recipient with male donor shows XY blood cells
Blood group can change to the donor type after transplant
Donor-derived T cells can cause graft-versus-host disease
Mixed chimerism signals incomplete engraftment or relapse

stem: A researcher studies a protein hormone made in the liver. Injecting it into mice raises platelet counts.
oneliner: Liver-made protein hormone raises platelets → where does it act?
ask: Where does this hormone bind to act?

options.B: On the cell membrane of megakaryocytes
options.C: In the cytoplasm of megakaryocytes
options.D: On the cell membrane of hepatocytes

whyNot.A: Only **steroid or thyroid** hormones act inside the nucleus
whyNot.C: Cytosolic receptors bind **lipid-soluble** hormones; a protein cannot cross the membrane
whyNot.D: The liver **makes** it; the target is the platelet precursor
whyNot.E: Wrong cell **and** wrong location for a peptide hormone

answer: On the cell membrane of megakaryocytes
why: **Thrombopoietin** is a **peptide hormone**, so it cannot enter cells and binds a **surface receptor (c-Mpl)** on **megakaryocytes** and platelet precursors, driving platelet production through JAK2.

idea.rule: Peptide hormones act on cell-surface receptors; steroid and thyroid hormones act on intracellular receptors.
also: EPO binds a surface receptor on erythroid progenitors
G-CSF binds a surface receptor on myeloid progenitors
Insulin receptor is a surface tyrosine kinase
Glucagon uses a surface G protein-coupled receptor

stem: A 44-year-old woman with chronic kidney disease has a persistent normocytic anemia. After she starts recombinant erythropoietin, her hemoglobin climbs because her marrow precursors make heme faster. The first committed step of that pathway, which heme itself normally switches off, is up-regulated.
oneliner: 44F + CKD anemia + erythropoietin + Hb rising + first committed step of heme synthesis up → which substrates?
ask: Which pair of compounds is condensed in the reaction that was stimulated?

options.C: Glycine and succinyl-CoA

whyNot.A: That is the **last** step (ferrochelatase), not the first committed step that heme feeds back on
whyNot.B: That joins two ALA molecules into porphobilinogen, a **later** step (ALA dehydratase)
whyNot.D: That begins **ketone body and cholesterol** synthesis, not heme
whyNot.E: That belongs to the **urea cycle**, not erythroid heme synthesis

answer: Glycine and succinyl-CoA (ALA synthase)
why: **ALA synthase** condenses **glycine with succinyl-CoA** in mitochondria to make aminolevulinic acid. It is the **rate-limiting, committed step** of heme synthesis, needs **pyridoxal phosphate (B6)**, is inhibited by heme and rises when erythroid demand rises.
chain: Erythropoietin or blood loss raises demand for heme
ALA is made, then fed into the later steps to heme
Heme feeds back to switch the enzyme off

idea.rule: The committed, rate-limiting step of a pathway is the one that is regulated.
also: Acetyl-CoA carboxylase in fatty acid synthesis
HMG-CoA reductase in cholesterol synthesis
Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I in the urea cycle
PFK-1 in glycolysis

stem: A 40-year-old man who drinks heavily and has chronic hepatitis C develops fragile skin with blisters and erosions on the backs of both hands after time in the sun. There is scarring, patchy darkening and excess facial hair, but he has had no abdominal or neurologic attacks. His urine is tea-colored and glows pink-orange under a Wood's lamp.
oneliner: 40M + alcohol + hepatitis C + blisters on sun-exposed hands + scarring + fluorescent tea-colored urine, no attacks → how are the skin lesions produced?
ask: Which mechanism most directly produces his skin lesions?

options.A: UVB-induced pyrimidine dimers in keratinocyte DNA
options.C: Absent melanin because of a tyrosinase defect
options.D: Stored pigment that absorbs light and makes free radicals

whyNot.A: UVB dimers underlie **sunburn and skin cancer**; his **fluorescent urine** points to a stored light-absorbing pigment
whyNot.B: Hemidesmosome antibodies cause **bullous pemphigoid**, which is not sun-triggered and gives no **fluorescent urine**
whyNot.C: A tyrosinase defect gives **albinism** (pale skin), not blisters with **patchy darkening**
whyNot.E: Defective excision repair is **xeroderma pigmentosum**, which does not make the **urine fluoresce**

answer: Light-absorbing porphyrins in the skin generating reactive oxygen species
why: In **porphyria cutanea tarda** (uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase deficiency) **porphyrins accumulate in the skin**. They absorb visible light, release **reactive oxygen species** and blister sun-exposed skin, with **no neurovisceral attacks**. Alcohol, hepatitis C and iron overload are triggers.
chain: Uroporphyrin builds up in liver, blood and skin
Reactive oxygen species damage the skin
Blisters, fragility and scarring on the hands

idea.rule: Late porphyrins cause light sensitivity; early precursors (ALA, PBG) cause neurovisceral attacks.
also: Erythropoietic protoporphyria: painful photosensitivity without blisters
Congenital erythropoietic porphyria: severe blistering from childhood
Acute intermittent porphyria: raised ALA and PBG, attacks but no photosensitivity
Variegate porphyria and hereditary coproporphyria: both attacks and blisters

stem: A 27-year-old woman develops swelling of the left calf and then chest pain with breathlessness the day after a long-haul flight. Imaging confirms a deep vein thrombosis with a pulmonary embolus. Her sister had a leg clot at 30. Protein C and protein S levels are normal, but an activated protein C resistance assay is abnormal.
oneliner: 27F + DVT and PE after long flight + sister with clot + normal protein C and S + abnormal APC resistance assay → which defect?
ask: Which molecular defect most likely explains her clots?

options.A: Factor Va that activated protein C cannot cleave
options.B: Low protein C so factors Va and VIIIa stay active
options.C: Low protein S, the cofactor of activated protein C
options.D: Excess prothrombin from a 3' untranslated variant

whyNot.B: Her **protein C level is normal**, so the problem is the target, not the enzyme
whyNot.C: Her **protein S level is normal**
whyNot.D: More prothrombin raises clot risk but does not make her plasma **resist activated protein C**
whyNot.E: Her **sister's clot at 30** points to an inherited defect, and the specific test abnormal is **APC resistance**

answer: Factor V Leiden: factor Va resistant to activated protein C
why: **Factor V Leiden** (Arg506Gln) makes factor Va **resistant to cleavage by activated protein C**. Thrombin generation continues unchecked, so **venous clots** form, often with a provoking factor such as travel. Protein C and S levels are **normal**, and the APC resistance assay is abnormal.
chain: Activated protein C cannot cleave factor Va
Factor Va stays active, thrombin keeps forming

idea.rule: Inherited thrombophilia = too much procoagulant activity or too little anticoagulant activity.
also: Factor V Leiden: factor Va resists activated protein C (commonest in White populations)
Prothrombin G20210A: more prothrombin made
Protein C or S deficiency: Va and VIIIa not inactivated; warfarin skin necrosis
Antithrombin deficiency: heparin raises the aPTT poorly

stem: A 52-year-old man with acute leukemia and a very high blast count has pain and swelling in the right ankle three days after his first chemotherapy cycle. He then notices blood in his urine and his creatinine rises. Potassium and phosphate are high and calcium is low.
oneliner: 52M + acute leukemia, high blast count + day 3 of chemotherapy + ankle pain + hematuria + high K and phosphate, low Ca → which crystal?
ask: Which crystal is most likely responsible for his joint and kidney injury?

options.C: Calcium pyrophosphate

whyNot.A: Oxalate stones follow **fat malabsorption or ethylene glycol**, not mass tumor-cell breakdown
whyNot.B: Cystine crystals need an **inherited transport defect**, not cell lysis after chemotherapy
whyNot.C: Pyrophosphate deposition is not caused by **cell lysis**; the timing after chemotherapy points to nucleic acid breakdown
whyNot.D: Struvite needs a **urease-producing infection**; his trigger is **massive tumor-cell death**

answer: Uric acid crystals
why: Chemotherapy lyses the tumor cells, releasing nucleic acids that are broken down from **purines to xanthine to uric acid**. **Uric acid crystallizes** in the tubules (hematuria, renal failure) and the joints (gout-like pain). The released phosphate also binds calcium and gives **hypocalcemia**.
chain: Uric acid crystals in tubules and joints
Acute kidney injury and gouty arthritis

idea.rule: Tumor lysis gives hyperkalemia, hyperphosphatemia, hyperuricemia and hypocalcemia.
also: Prevent with hydration plus allopurinol or rasburicase
Rasburicase breaks uric acid down to allantoin
Highest risk: Burkitt lymphoma and acute leukemias
Allopurinol inhibits xanthine oxidase

stem: In a flow-chamber experiment, platelets are perfused over a stretch of vessel wall stripped of endothelium so that collagen is exposed. Platelets normally stick under high shear. When one plasma protein is removed, they no longer adhere, although platelet glycoprotein Ib and collagen are intact. The same protein also carries factor VIII in plasma.
oneliner: Experiment: platelets over exposed collagen + adhesion lost when one plasma protein removed + same protein carries factor VIII → which protein?
ask: Which plasma protein was removed?

options.C: Thrombomodulin

whyNot.A: Fibrinogen bridges **GPIIb/IIIa** during later aggregation and does not carry factor VIII
whyNot.C: Thrombomodulin is on endothelium and **activates protein C**; it is not a plasma bridge
whyNot.D: Tissue factor starts the **extrinsic** coagulation pathway and is not a platelet bridge
whyNot.E: Spectrin is an **intracellular** red cell membrane protein, not in plasma

answer: von Willebrand factor
why: Platelet adhesion needs **von Willebrand factor** to bridge **exposed subendothelial collagen to platelet glycoprotein Ib**. It also carries and protects **factor VIII**. Fibrinogen acts later, linking platelets through GPIIb/IIIa in aggregation.

idea.rule: Adhesion uses vWF and GPIb; aggregation uses fibrinogen and GPIIb/IIIa.
also: Bernard-Soulier: absent GPIb, giant platelets
Glanzmann thrombasthenia: absent GPIIb/IIIa
von Willebrand disease: long bleeding time, may have low factor VIII
Ristocetin cofactor assay tests vWF-GPIb binding

stem: A 57-year-old woman has a 1.3-cm breast lump. A core biopsy shows invasive carcinoma. The pathologist is asked to assign the tumor a grade rather than a stage.
oneliner: 57F + 1.3-cm breast mass + biopsy: carcinoma + asked to grade (not stage) → which feature?
ask: Which feature is used in grading this carcinoma?

options.C: Presence of distant metastasis
options.E: Number of mitoses per unit area

whyNot.A: Size is the **T** of TNM staging
whyNot.B: Nodal spread is the **N** of TNM staging
whyNot.C: Metastasis is the **M** of TNM staging
whyNot.D: A host response is not part of the **tumor-cell grading** system

answer: Number of mitoses per unit area
why: **Grade** describes how the tumor cells look: **differentiation, nuclear pleomorphism and mitotic count**. A high mitotic rate reflects rapid division and a **high-grade**, poorly differentiated tumor. **Stage** uses size, nodes and metastasis (TNM).

idea.rule: Grade = how the cells look; stage = how far the tumor has spread.
also: Breast cancer grading uses tubule formation, nuclear grade and mitoses
Poorly differentiated tumors are high grade
TNM stage usually predicts prognosis better than grade
Gleason score is prostate grading
